text: Skin lesion classification
Project review: models, methods and findings
Academic research prototype
Project scope: README.md. This is a research prototype, not a clinical diagnostic system.
The problem and project goal
Skin images contain visual patterns that can help classify seven lesion types.
Training data is imbalanced, and patient images raise privacy concerns.
Our goal: compare image models and explore privacy-preserving training.
Sources: README.md; TRAINING.md. The federated and centralized feature experiments are separate.
Research that shaped the work
PanDerm: a dermatology foundation encoder can transfer to lesion classification with a trained head.
Multi-scale CNN research motivated looking at images in multiple views.
Published scores use different datasets, splits and metrics, so direct rankings can mislead.

Sources: Yan et al., https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-03747-y; Mahbod et al., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32268255/; data/reference/research_papers.json. PanDerm published weighted F1 is not macro F1.
Dataset and evaluation
HAM10000: 10,015 dermoscopic images across seven diagnoses.
Our internal split: 7,014 training, 1,509 validation and 1,492 test images.
Images of the same lesion stay together within these internal splits.
Separate ISIC sets: 193 validation and 1,512 test images.
Sources: TRAINING.md; outputs/feature_models/efficientnet_b0/REPORT.md. Official sets do not supply lesion IDs, so cross-set lesion separation cannot be established.
What the models see
Dermoscopic images vary in color, shape and texture.
The model learns visual features from images, then predicts one of seven classes.

Examples from data/raw/images/ISIC_0024306.jpg, ISIC_0024307.jpg and ISIC_0024308.jpg. Images come from HAM10000; examples are illustrative and are not shown as a diagnosis. Dataset citation: https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2018.161.
Our model workflow
1   Prepare images and split by lesion
2   Extract features with a pretrained image encoder
3   Train and select a classifier using training and validation data
4   Evaluate saved models on held-out sets and inspect class-level results
Sources: TRAINING.md; outputs/feature_models/panderm_large_comparison/REPORT.md. Large uses the authors’ released split, rather than the original internal split.

Early   Centralized and federated CNN prototype; EfficientNet feature baselines
Next   Class balancing, multiple views and lesion-specific classifiers
Then   Frozen PanDerm Base with linear, neural and XGBoost heads

EfficientNet-B0 experiments
A pretrained ImageNet encoder converts each image into reusable features.
Compared logistic regression, a neural network and XGBoost.
Tested class weighting, SMOTE and multi-view image features.
Also trained a separate fine-tuned EfficientNet CNN; its recorded run lasted 15 epochs.

Sources: TRAINING.md; outputs/feature_models/efficientnet_b0_improved/REPORT.md; outputs/cnn_baseline/efficientnet_b0_finetuned/history.json and protocol.json. Recorded epoch durations sum to approximately 21.8 minutes, excluding setup. Fine-tuning and frozen features are separate experiments.

What the EfficientNet experiments showed
Original neural head: 61.6% internal test macro F1.
Improved multi-view linear head: 61.5% macro F1 on the official test.
SMOTE helped some heads but reduced XGBoost macro F1 in the original comparison.
Seven specialist classifiers did not beat the improved linear model overall.

Sources: outputs/feature_models/efficientnet_b0/REPORT.md; outputs/feature_models/efficientnet_b0_improved/REPORT.md; outputs/feature_models/efficientnet_b0_specialists/REPORT.md. Different test sets are labeled explicitly.
PanDerm: why we tested it
PanDerm is pretrained for dermatology, while EfficientNet starts with general ImageNet features.
We froze the encoder and trained small classifiers on its image embeddings.
Base produces 768 features per image; Large produces 1,024.
A bare encoder cannot predict seven diagnoses without a trained readout.
Sources: outputs/feature_models/panderm_base_comparison/REPORT.md; outputs/feature_models/panderm_large_comparison/REPORT.md; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-03747-y.

PanDerm Base and Large results
Base + neural head: 70.3% macro F1 on the 1,512-image official test.
Large + linear head: 73.8% macro F1 on the same official test.
Large + author-style probe: 71.6% macro F1 on that official test.
Training splits and head selection differ, so this is not an encoder-only comparison.

Sources: outputs/feature_models/panderm_base_comparison/REPORT.md; outputs/feature_models/panderm_large_comparison/REPORT.md; outputs/diagnostics/panderm_paper_reference/REPORT.md. Base trained on 7,014 images; Large used 8,207 authors’ released training images. Tests had previously been examined.
PanDerm Large: model comparison
Author-style probe: 80.98% macro F1 on the released HAM test.
Smaller neural head (192–64): 81.73% macro F1 on the same test.
Linear head led the shown Large models on official-test macro F1: 73.80%.
Wider or more complex heads did not consistently improve every test set.

Sources: outputs/feature_models/panderm_large_refined/REPORT.md; outputs/feature_models/panderm_large_capacity/REPORT.md. Released HAM test contains 1,232 images. Reused test results are exploratory; they are not fresh independent confirmation.
Privacy-preserving workflow
The federated prototype simulates separate clients that train locally.
A server combines model updates into a shared model using FedAvg or FedProx.
Optional differential privacy adds noise during local training.
The feature-model results shown here are centralized and do not claim DP.

Sources: README.md; config.yaml; src/client/client.py; src/server/strategy.py. Differential privacy accounting covers training-image updates, not a patient-level guarantee. Simulation is not evidence of real multi-hospital deployment.

What we learned
Macro F1 matters because it gives rare lesion classes equal weight.
PanDerm features improved the reported official-test results in our experiments.
Specialists and larger heads can overfit or improve one split while losing on another.
The authors’ published weighted F1 and our macro F1 measure different things.

Limitations and next steps
Repeated examination of test sets makes the comparisons exploratory.
Later adaptation used former test images for training; those scores are fitting results.
Evaluate a locked model on a fresh, independent dataset with lesion identifiers.
Test privacy and utility together before claiming a private clinical model.

Sources: outputs/diagnostics/panderm_test_adaptation_once/REPORT.md; outputs/diagnostics/six_model_adaptation/REPORT.md; README.md; TRAINING.md. Pretraining overlap with downstream datasets has not been independently excluded.
Project review: key conclusion
We built an end-to-end research workflow for seven-class lesion classification.
The project compared EfficientNet and PanDerm with several classifier families.
PanDerm Large with a linear head reached 73.8% macro F1 on the official test.
A fresh independent evaluation is needed before any clinical conclusion.
Sources: README.md; outputs/feature_models/panderm_large_comparison/REPORT.md. The reported official-test score is exploratory after repeated test inspection.
